newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Abkhaz separatist poll goes ahead despite violence.
newsitem.headline: Abkhaz separatist poll goes ahead despite violence.

text.p: Sporadic fighting and a series of explosions on Saturday overshadowed a parliamentary election in Georgia's breakaway region of Abkhazia, denounced by Tbilisi, Moscow and the West.

An Abkhaz Interior Ministry official said Georgian partisans armed with grenade launchers and automatic weapons launched cross-border attacks in the eastern region of Gali, the only part of Abkhazia predominantly populated by ethnic Georgians.
He said one Abkhaz policeman had been injured in a two-pronged attack in a border village.

Abkhaz leader Vladislav Ardzinba said the violence was inspired by the Georgian government of Eduard Shevardnadze. "I am lodging a firm protest. This is what the Georgians call democracy," he said of the attacks after casting his ballot.
Tbilisi says the vote is illegal but has denied any links with the alleged "sabotage units".
"Those seeking now a place on a bench of the parliament (in Abkhazia) will shortly take place in the dock," said a commentator on the Georgian television.

Gali was tense and mostly elderly ethnic Georgians were voting. While they said they were doing so voluntarily, some townspeople said residents were afraid of Abkhaz retribution if they did not cast ballots.

About 10 armed Abkhazians guarded one polling station and voters were handed ballots with a single candidate listed. There was no voting booth and an election official sat directly behind the ballot box.

"They are afraid the Georgians will punish them if they do vote and afraid the Abkhaz will if they don't. Since they are here in Abkhazia, they have to be more afraid of the Abkhaz," said a local woman selling cheese pies in a street cafe.
Blue-helmeted Russian peacekeepers cruised the streets in armoured vehicles and Abkhaz fighters combed the town for mines, formerly home to 60,000 people.

In other parts of Abkhazia voting was proceeding smoothly and the turnout appeared strong. The central electoral commission said 71 percent of 219,000 eligible voters had cast ballots by 4 p.m. (1300 GMT), making the election valid.
A steady stream of people began arriving at one central polling place in Sukhumi just after polls opened at 7 a.m. (0400GMT).
A long hall was decked out in green, red and white Abkhaz flags and portraits of separatist fighters killed in the bitter 1992-93 conflict with Georgian troops.

Some residents said they were encouraged by the nearby Chechnya's battle for independence from Russia. "Chechnya proved it could win its independence. We hope that means one day Georgia will let us be free too," said 78-year-old Vera Kazakova after voting.

As the Soviet Union disintegrated, many in Abkhazia began clamouring for independence. The Georgians and the Abkhaz share many cultural traditions but speak different languages and relations have often been strained.

Abkhazia, a Black Sea coastal region once favoured by the Soviet communist elite, has run itself as an independent state since 1993 when its fighters routed Georgian government troops after a year-long war which cost 10,000 lives.
At least 150,000 ethnic Georgian refugees have still not returned to Abkhazia after they fled the conflict.
Georgia wants them to be allowed to return home and for political issues to be resolved before any elections.
The refugees take part in a parallel plebiscite organised by Tbilisi on Saturday in which they will get a chance to condemn the vote, going on without them, as illegitimate.
The U.N. and the European Union and the Georgian government have called for the cancellation of the Abkhaz election, in which 81 candidates are vying for 35 parliamentary seats.
